sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The traditional distribution network relay protection mainly relies on the high short-
circuit current, which is nearly 10–20 times the normal current value to detect the fault and
disconnect the fault feeder. The high short-circuit current is generated by the system-side
rotating synchronous generator [1]. And then, the distribution automation remote terminal
units (DRTUs) are used to realize the fault section localization and fault isolation according
to the inherent local logic action [ 2]. These abovementioned strategies can guarantee
the safe and reliable operation of the distribution system in case of faults of the power
distribution line.
With the increasing proportion of renewable sources’ access to the distribution net-
work, traditional short-circuit current calculation results cannot reveal the real-time short-
circuit variation characteristics and cannot provide theoretical knowledge to obtain the
reasonable setting calculation of relay protection, as well as the parameter selection of
power equipment, such as circuit breakers. It has been shown that the output short-circuit
current of a renewable source is completely determined by its control strategy and control
parameters, and its short-circuit current is restricted, distorted, and unable to provide
significantly increased current characteristics [ 3–5]. However, due to the secrecy of the
manufacturers and the variable operating environment in the field, it is impossible to accu-
rately know the control strategy and parameters of all grid-connected converter devices. In
the meantime, the number of distributed generators (DGs) in the distribution network is
Appl. Sci. 2024, 14, 11001. https://doi.org/10.3390/app142311001 https://www.mdpi.com/journal/applsci
Appl. Sci. 2024, 14, 11001 2 of 22
large and widely dispersed, and it is impossible to accurately take into account the control
characteristics of the renewable sources to calculate the short-circuit current [6]. Therefore,
most of the existing short-circuit current calculations used in the field equate the equivalent
output short-circuit current of DGs to zero or the maximum rated value [7–9], which leads
to a large error in the calculation of the short-circuit current of the whole network, and
there is a risk of erroneous rejection of the distribution network protection.
A lot of research work has been carried out by scholars on the calculation of short-
circuit current considering partial-power inverter-type and full-power-type DGs under
different voltage drop conditions caused by grid faults. Among them, the output current of
partial-power inverter-type DGs is mainly calculated via the voltage drop at the terminal,
and the crowbar action would also affect the output current if the voltage dip reaches a
predefined threshold [10–12]. Different from partial-power inverter-type DGs, the output
current of full-power inverter-type DGs relies entirely on the control of grid-connected
inverters [13–15]. The results show that the output fault current of a single distributed
renewable energy resource is characterized by a segmented function of the terminal voltage
during a grid fault. In refs. [16–18], the approximate equivalent expressions of the short-
circuit current are derived from the mechanism of the control strategies of the partial-power
inverter-type DGs before and after the grid fault, and the results have been verified in the
recorded field data. Similar work has also been carried out for full-power inverter-type
DGs in the literature [19–21]. Although the analysis of full-time short-circuit currents of
partial-power and full-power inverter-type DGs during grid faults is not yet able to meet
the actual and complicated recorded transient waves in the field, the modeling and analysis
of their output steady-state fault currents have been relatively mature, which can satisfy the
calculation of short-circuit currents of distribution networks under some constant scene.
Accordingly, scholars have proposed an iterative method for short-circuit calculation
of distribution networks containing renewable DGs [22–24] to fully take into account the
influence of the strong coupling relationship between the fault current of DGs and the
voltage at the point of common coupling (PCC). In these methods, the initial voltage
values of all buses in the distribution network after the fault is obtained via traditional
short-circuit current calculation methods, in which the DGs are regarded as ideal current or
voltage sources. And then, the change in the node voltage caused by the output current
of DGs under LVRT strategies is repetitively and iteratively calculated to form the final
short-circuit current of each branch of the distribution network. The calculation results in
these papers show that the accuracy of short circuit current calculation can be improved by
10% compared with the traditional simplified methods.
In fact, the output power of renewable DGs has strong randomness [25–27], and the
average hourly output in 24 h is not the same. Hence, the node voltage has strong volatility
during normal daily operation of the distribution network. The calculation of short-circuit
current according to the rated power output of DGs is not in line with the actual situation
and affects the sensitivity calibration of over-current protection. In other words, the node
voltage along the feeder varies with the output power of DGs and the electricity loads.
Hence, the short-circuit current in electrical distribution systems should be calculated based
on the real-time operation conditions of the distribution network.
To address the abovementioned problems, existing short-circuit current calculation
methods are analyzed for the distribution network with renewable DGs. And then, the
daily output power of PV stations is analyzed, clustered, and modeled for the real-time
power flow calculation of distribution networks, as well as the residential loads. Once
the node voltage value before the fault time is obtained in real time by considering the
source-load stochasticity, an improved iterative short-circuit current calculation algorithm
is proposed and verified considering high penetration of DGs with LVRT strategies. The
main contributions of this paper are given as follows:
• An improved iterative short-circuit current calculation algorithm is proposed consid-
ering real-time output power of DGs and electricity loads under high penetration of
DGs with LVRT strategies;
Appl. Sci. 2024, 14, 11001 3 of 22
• Output power fluctuation analysis of PV stations of residential loads are conducted
via clustering algorithms. Several typical daily curves of PV stations and electricity
loads are obtained and used to obtain the typical daily short-circuit current curves for
all branches.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces a traditional
simplified short-circuit current calculation in a distribution network with renewable DGs,
including the equivalent short-circuit analysis networks, equivalent model of renewable
DGs for short-circuit calculation, and the corresponding calculation equations. Section 3
provides a detailed illustration of our proposed real-time short-circuit current calculation
considering fluctuation in DGs and loads. Section 4 presents the analysis and verification
short-circuit results of a 69-node distribution network with different scales of PV stations
using our proposed method and traditional calculation methods. Section 5 summarizes the
research findings and discusses future prospects.

sections.title: 2.2 Short-Circuit Current Calculation for Distribution Networks with Renewable DGs
sections.text:
There are three general methods to calculate the short-circuit current of distribution
networks containing renewable DGs.
In the first-type methods, the output current of all renewable DGs is regarded as
zero in the short-circuit current calculation. In these methods, the influence of DGs on
the short-circuit is ignored in the calculation. Since the output current of all DGs equals
zero, the voltage of each node can be obtained via a power flow calculation, and then, the
short-circuit current can be calculated based on Equation (7).
In the second-type methods, the output current of all renewable DGs is regarded as
1.2 times the rated current in the short-circuit current calculation. The voltage at each node
during normal operation of the distribution network is calculated under the condition of a
rated output current of all renewable DGs, and then, the short-circuit voltage at each node
and short-circuit current in each branch circuit is calculated with 1.2 times the rated output
current of all DGs after a fault occurs at the fault point.
In the third-type methods, the output current of renewable DGs is calculated ac-
cording to the real value under LVRT strategies. The detailed processes are given as the
following steps:
Step 1: according to the real-time output of the renewable DGs, the voltage of all nodes
is obtained via a traditional power flow calculation before the fault occurred. And then, the

Step 4: steps 2 and 3 are carried out iteratively until the difference value of the voltage
at each node in two consecutive calculation is less than a threshold value. And then,
the output current of DGs and the voltage at each node can be obtained, as well as the
short-circuit current of each branch circuit.

sections.title: 2.3 Equivalent Model of Renewable DGs for Short-Circuit Calculation
sections.text:
In the short-circuit calculation of the AC power grid with renewable DGs, the equiv-
alent model of DGs is usually analyzed according to the voltage drop of the PCC point,
whether for the distributed access of a single DG to the AC power grid or the centralized
access of large-scale DGs to the AC power grid. Common DGs in distribution networks can
be generally divided into two categories according to the type of grid connection control
strategy, including a doubly fed induction generator (DFIG) belonging to the part-power
inverter-based power sources and photovoltaic sources and a permanent-magnet direct-
drive wind turbine belonging to full-power inverter-based distributed generators (IIDGs).
Since the control strategies of a DFIG and IIDG are different, the equivalent models need to
be discussed separately.
When the voltage drop value at the grid point of a DFIG is big, about 0.2–0.4 p.u. of the
rated voltage, the crowbar protection is put into operation to avoid the rotor inrush current.
And then, the DFIG is equivalent to the induction motor after the crowbar resistance is
strung; the short-circuit current and the voltage at the grid point are linearly correlated.
When the voltage drop value is limited, about 0.4–0.9 p.u., the crowbar resistance is not
put into use, and the reactive output current would be adaptively regulated via the control
system according to the voltage drop value at the terminal of DGs. The above output
characteristics of a DFIG are summarized as a mathematical expression in the form of
a segmented function, which can be equated to mode 1 and mode 2 by analyzing the
results of various research scholars, as shown in Equations (10) and (11), respectively.
The difference between Equations (10) and (11) is in the treatment of the intermediate
nonlinearization intervals when the voltage of the PCC is in the range of [0.2 0.9] p.u.
Different from Equation (10), the saturation current of the inverter, which is limited by
the current carrying capacity of the power electronic devices, is specially considered in
Equation (11). In the meantime, the normal output active current, IN, is also considered in
Equation (11), while only the reactive current is considered in Equation (10).
According to refs. [28,29], the equivalent modes of a DFIG for output current calcula-
tion can be expressed with Equations (10) and (11), while the equivalent mode of an IIDG
is expressed with Equation (12).

sections.title: 3 Short-Circuit Current Calculation Considering Power Fluctuation
3.1 Output Power Fluctuation Analysis of PV Stations
sections.text:
Among the DGs in distribution network, distributed photovoltaic stations (PVs) are
dominant, and different PVs in the same distribution grid usually have a consistency, which
corresponds to the intensity of solar radiation. The Ausgrid dataset can be obtained from
the official website [30]. The historical data include output power curves of nearly three
hundred household rooftop photovoltaic system. The yearly output power of the rooftop
photovoltaic system of customer 2 is selected by us for the analysis and clustering. Based on
the Ausgrid dataset, the distributed rooftop PV output is converted to standardized output
data at half-hour intervals, and the PV output characteristics of single-family residents are
shown in Figure 2.
As shown in Figure 2, the PV power output in all four seasons of spring, summer, fall,
and winter have obvious randomness. Cluster analysis of the output curves shows that
the distributed PV output is the largest from 10:00 to 14:00, when the corresponding light
intensity is also the largest. This is a typical sunny day output characteristic, but there is
also a more obvious volatility on a daily basis. Other categories of PV output are irregular,
depending on the environmental factors during the day.

3.3. Real-Time Short-Circuit Current Calculation Considering Fluctuation in DGs and Loads 
Based on the abovementioned analysis, it can be seen that the DGs and loads at each 
node of the distribution network ha ve a strong randomness due to the in ﬂuence of solar 
radiation and electricity consumption pa tterns. Their in ﬂuence on the distribution net-
work short-circuit current calculation can be summarized as follows: 
(1) In the short-circuit calculation, the node voltage value before the fault time should be 
obtained in real time by considering the source-load stochasticity, which cannot be 
simpliﬁed to the rated voltage. It can be derived that the voltage changed because of 
the volatility in DGs and loads at each node of the distribution network throughout 
the day and 24 h. In the meantime, the short-circuit current of each branch is directly 
determined via the voltage at each node after the fault based on Equation (7); 
(2) In the short-circuit calculation, DGs in distribution networks can be equivalent to 
voltage-controlled current sources according to the LVRT strategies. According to 
Equations (10)–(12), the output current of DGs after the fault will change from the 
output current at the pre-fault moment. If the output current of a DG at the node j 
before and after the fault changed by ΔIIIDG,j, this updated injected current ΔIIIDG,j is

(1) In the short-circuit calculation, the node voltage value before the fault time should be
obtained in real time by considering the source-load stochasticity, which cannot be

sections.text:

Newton–Raphson power flow calculation. And then, MATLAB code is written by us to
realize the continuous power flow calculation using the clustered daily curves of DGs and
electricity loads. Finally, Equations (5)–(7) and (13)–(16) mentioned in our procedures are

Figure 8. Voltage at some selected nodes on sunny days during 24 h: (a) node 27; (b) node 54. 
As shown in Figure 8, the voltage at node s 27 and 54 change with the fluctuation in 
loads during 24 h in a whole day. Take node 27 in the first case as an example, which is 
shown in Figure 8a: the lowest voltage reaches 0.956 p.u. at 20:00, while its highest voltage 
reaches 0.980 p.u. at 4:00, nearly 1.025 times the lowest voltage value. In the meantime, due 
to the output power of distributed DGs, the voltages at node 27 in the second case and third 
case are obviously different from that in the first case. At 13:00, the voltage at node 27 in the 
first case, second case, and third case, is 0.9721, 0.9922, 0.9927, respectively. In other words, 
the voltage at some node may change 2.1% because of the output power of DGs. In addition, 
the voltages at some nodes in the second case are different from that at the same node in the 
third case. Take node 54 as an example, which is shown in Figure 8b: at 14:00, the voltage at 
node 54 in the first case, second case, and third case is 0.9453, 0.9508, 0.9585, respectively.
